title: Identifying phase separation modulators mediated by the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein using a structure-based drug discovery approach.
authors: Du, Shaoqing; Jang, Yejin; Hu, Xueping; Li, Ping; Wang, Bo; Ra, Hyun Su; Kang, Dongwei; Wang, Xiaolong; Wang, Nonghan; Liu, Xinyong; Kim, Meehyein; Zhan, Peng
abstract: INTRODUCTION: As severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) continues to evolve through mutations and acquire resistance to existing antiviral agents, the persistence of post-pandemic infections remains a significant global health concern. To address these challenges, it is crucial to develop novel therapeutic agents that target previously unexplored viral or host mechanisms. OBJECTIVES: The nucleocapsid (N) protein of SARS-CoV-2 plays a critical role in viral RNA replication and genome packaging through its ability to undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). Targeting the condensation of N-RNA complex could potentially serve as an effective therapeutic strategy against coronavirus infections. The present study provides a successful exemplification of antiviral agent discovery by targeting the viral N protein on the basis of its structural characteristics. METHODS: A total of 23 virtual screening compounds and 16 hit derivatives were prepared. Their binding affinity and antiviral activities were evaluated using surface plasmon resonance and immunofluorescence assay, respectively. The impact of these compounds on condensate formation was verified through fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, as well as the inhibition of N condensate formation in cells. RESULTS: Structure-based virtual screening, target protein binding affinity quantification, and cell culture-based anti-SARS-CoV-2 assays enabled the identification a hit compound, D21. Subsequent structural optimization of series I and II yielded compound II8, which exhibits stronger binding affinity for the N protein and effectively inhibits the formation of N-RNA condensates, thereby demonstrating its potential to modulate LLPS, a mechanism underlying its antiviral activity. In vivo evaluation showed that II8 displays antiviral activity in a human ACE2-expressing mouse model when administered intranasally as a pre-incubated mixture with SARS-CoV-2. Due to the pharmacokinetic profile of compound II8, further structural modifications are still required. CONCLUSION: Our findings suggest that compound II8 may serve as a localized prophylactic nasal spray, providing valuable insights for further development of LLPS modulators as next-generation antiviral agents.

title: RNA Synthesis and Degradation Regulate Biomolecular Condensates through Nonequilibrium Feedback.
authors: Sanchez-Burgos, Ignacio; Tejedor, Andres R; Ocana, Alberto; Espinosa, Jorge R; Collepardo-Guevara, Rosana
abstract: Transcriptional condensates operate far from equilibrium, where continuous RNA synthesis and degradation dynamically reshape condensate composition. To investigate how RNA synthesis regulates condensate properties at submolecular resolution, we introduce REACT-RNA, a chemically specific coarse-grained molecular dynamics framework that explicitly couples RNA polymerization, degradation, and nucleotide fluxes to sequence-dependent protein-RNA phase behavior and apply it to FUS and MED1 condensates. We find that RNA polymerization occurs preferentially at condensate interfaces because interfaces promote a highly reactive microenvironment that combines nucleotide influx, enrichment of reactive RNA chain ends, and enhanced molecular dynamics. Interfacial RNA polymerization generates a spatially organized RNA population, with newly synthesized short RNAs enriched near the interface and longer RNAs partitioning toward the condensate core, which decreases the interfacial free energy and promotes multivalent RNA-protein interactions. As RNA concentration and chain length evolve over time, condensate composition, density, and stability change dynamically in response. Sustained RNA polymerization drives re-entrant condensate dissolution, even of aged gel-like condensates, whereas RNA degradation stabilizes long-lived nonequilibrium condensates containing elevated RNA content. Our results suggest that RNA synthesis, degradation, and nucleotide fluxes drive transcriptional condensates out of thermodynamic equilibrium, while condensates in turn promote reactive molecular configurations that favor RNA production, enabling transient accumulation of RNA-rich compositional imbalance during bursts of transcription.

title: Heterogeneity-aware structure-sequence expert collaboration for RNA-binding site prediction with evidence-grounded interpretation.
authors: Mi, Jia; Wang, Han; Li, Jing; Wan, Jing; Wang, Kunfeng
abstract: RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) play central roles in post-transcriptional regulation. However, accurately predicting their RNA-binding sites remains challenging due to two issues. First, pronounced heterogeneity between structured domains and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) within RBP sequences makes residue-level binding site prediction difficult. Second, existing methods fail to provide candidate RNA ligands and their biological annotations for the query protein alongside predicted binding sites, leaving researchers without reference molecules for experimental follow-up. To address these two challenges, we propose a heterogeneity-aware structure-sequence expert collaboration framework with evidence-grounded interpretation for RNA-binding site prediction. Specifically, the proposed framework addresses the heterogeneity between structured domains and IDRs by training a Structural Expert and a Sequence Expert in a multi-stage manner to learn complementary structural and sequential representations for residue-level RNA-binding site prediction. In parallel, the proposed protein-RNA knowledge graph addresses the lack of biological evidence in existing methods by identifying proteins similar to the query protein and transferring their experimentally validated RNA ligands and associated biological annotations as candidate evidence for the query protein. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate improvements over representative baselines including MPBind, GPSite, and DeepPROBind, across several evaluation metrics. Together, the proposed framework combines heterogeneity-aware residue modeling with evidence-grounded interpretation, improving predictive performance while providing biologically supported candidate RNA ligands for downstream functional analysis and experimental validation. The source code is available at: https://github.com/MiJia-ID/KG-RNA.

title: Salt-Mediated Long-Range Electrostatic Signature of Native Binding Surface Pre-Organizes Bound-Like Conformations of p53 C-Terminal Intrinsically Disordered Region.
authors: Das, Kingshuk; Jana, Biman
journal: Chemphyschem : a European journal of chemical physics and physical chemistry
abstract: Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and regions (IDRs) often undergo a disorder-to-order transition via coupled folding and binding. The p53 C-terminal domain (CTD) IDR folds into a helical conformation upon binding S100B, yet the long-range influence of the ionic environment on this transition remains poorly understood. Using all-atom molecular dynamics simulations with a novel confinement setup, we investigated the conformational landscape of a 12-residue fragment of p53 CTD at varying distances from the S100B binding cleft. Comparing behavior in pure water and physiological salt (150 mM NaCl), we find that at 10 A from the native binding surface, the peptide spontaneously forms stable, bound-like helical segments exclusively in the salt solution. This effect is distance-dependent, vanishing at 20 A, and specific to the native binding surface, notably occurring without direct protein-IDR contacts. Our results demonstrate that the negatively charged S100B surface organizes solvated ions into a structured, long-range electrostatic microenvironment that thermodynamically stabilizes bound-like helical conformations prior to direct contact. This reveals a synergistic effect between native surface topology and physiological salt that biases the IDR's conformational ensemble to facilitate binding, identifying the ions in the solution as active participants in molecular recognition.

title: Valency-Limited Molecular Dynamics Simulations of Stickers-and-Spacers Polymers Reveal a Trade-Off between Condensation and Organization.
authors: Zhang, Yumeng; Sood, Amogh; Athreya, Advait; Zhang, Bin
journal: The journal of physical chemistry. B
abstract: Biomolecular condensates formed by intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are often described using stickers-and-spacers models, in which specific sticker motifs form reversible cross-links and spacer regions modulate phase behavior. Recent theory predicts that heterogeneous nonspecific spacer interactions can promote condensation but may also disrupt sticker-mediated organization. Here, we develop an off-lattice coarse-grained stickers-and-spacers polymer model for continuous molecular dynamics simulations and implement it in the GPU-accelerated OpenABC package. The model uses a directional sticker-sticker interaction to encode limited valency through interaction geometry, producing effectively one-to-one sticker binding without explicit bond assignment. Simulations of one-component systems show that sticker affinity and multivalency promote porous, network-like condensates, while nonspecific spacer interactions can also drive phase separation but produce more compact, spacer-dominated dense phases. When both interaction types are present, strong spacer heterogeneity reduces sticker conversion, suppresses sticker mobility, and disrupts the sticker-mediated network. In two-component systems, specific sticker interactions buffer client recruitment into host condensates, while nonspecific spacer interactions produce reservoir-dependent uptake. These results support a trade-off in which spacer heterogeneity promotes condensation at the cost of condensate organization and compositional robustness, providing a physical rationale for the suppression of promiscuous spacer interactions in low-complexity IDP regions.

title: Single-Chain Conformational Fluctuation Regulates Phase Separation of Intrinsically Disordered Proteins.
authors: Feng, Cibo; Xu, Shiqinrui; Su, Haibin; Chu, Xiakun
abstract: Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) form biomolecular condensates through weak multivalent interactions, but the ensemble variables that control condensate stability and material properties remain incompletely defined. Most current descriptions emphasize sequence features or mean single-chain descriptors, such as the radius of gyration R (g). Here, we ask whether the breadth of the single-chain ensemble can regulate liquid-liquid phase separation when the amino-acid sequence and mean chain size are fixed. We develop an all-atom-informed maximum-entropy coarse-grained model of the low-complexity domain of Fused in sarcoma (FUS-LCD) that preserves atomistic contact propensities while tuning the width of the isolated-chain R (g) distribution. This design yields dynamically quenched (Qch), middle (Mid), and flexible (Flx) models with nearly identical ⟨R (g)⟩ but increasing conformational fluctuation. Increasing fluctuation produces chains that are locally compact yet globally extensible, and decouples condensate density from thermodynamic stability: Flx forms a dense low-temperature phase but has lower critical temperature and surface tension. Flx condensates also show faster diffusion, shorter contact lifetimes, accelerated stress relaxation, delayed early nucleation, and faster late-stage coalescence. This more dynamic state also exhibits weaker orientational organization, with Flx showing the lowest orientational order among the three models. Our results identify single-chain conformational fluctuation as an ensemble-level control variable that links local IDP organization to condensate thermodynamics, transport, viscoelasticity, assembly, and mesoscopic order.

title: Proteases and proteolysis in biomolecular condensates.
authors: Moschou, Panagiotis N; Bozhkov, Peter V
abstract: Proteases have long been conceptualised as enzymes operating in dilute aqueous environments. Yet many localise to biomolecular condensates, which arise through phase separation. We argue that protease behaviour is governed by the condensate's physical regime: a dynamic liquid-like state, a surface-associated wetting layer, a slowed gel-like state, or a kinetically arrested solid. Each regime constrains protease kinetics, for example by slowing diffusion of protease and substrate. Activity can also be dictated by condensate composition rather than protease concentration alone: the local environment can alter substrate affinities, reshape enzyme conformational equilibria beyond bulk mass-action predictions, and buffer pH. Proteolysis need not occur in the dense phase; the interface can be an additional reaction compartment. Recent evidence suggests that condensates can hydrolyse substrates even without an enzyme, so cleavage attributed to a resident protease needs a catalytically inactive control to separate enzyme-catalysed proteolysis from condensate-mediated hydrolysis. Examining plant proteases through these lenses, we argue that the regimes themselves can be a consequence of proteolysis. Direct evidence linking proteases to condensate regulation, and vice versa, remains limited. Closing this gap will require regime-aware kinetics, phase-resolved measurements of dense-phase concentration, mobility and turnover, and falsifiable models integrating proteolysis with condensate physics.

title: Cooperative nature of residue interactions in biomolecular condensates.
authors: Chen, Le; Wu, Xiangyu; Hu, Guorong; Zeng, Xiangze; Li, Jingyuan
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: Cooperativity of residue interactions is prevalent in proteins and plays an essential role in protein folding. However, whether cooperativity exists in intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and their assembled biomolecular condensates remains elusive. Here, we reveal the presence of residue interaction cooperativity in various IDP condensates using atomistic molecular dynamics simulations. In all these condensates, cooperative residue interactions manifest as packing between finite residue motifs (3 to 5 residues) with lifetimes three orders of magnitude longer than residue contacts. Notably, these higher-order interactions (HOIs) exhibit a significant nonadditive free energy, which originates from a local low-dielectric environment. The underlying sequence patterns like "Y-X-Q", "D-X-R", and "S-Y-X" are identified. Furthermore, HOIs dominate the cohesive energy of IDPs and condensates can be treated as HOI-crosslinked networks. This model can successfully reproduce experimental results of condensate physical properties, including saturation concentration, viscoelasticity, and interfacial tension.

title: Charge density effect of micelles on liquid-liquid phase separation.
authors: Farshad, Mohsen; Baksi, Atanu; Whitmer, Jonathan K
abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) is central to the organization of biological and synthetic soft matter systems, yet how electrostatic interactions control condensation remains incompletely understood. Using coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we investigate LLPS in charged micelle-polymer mixtures, focusing on how micelle charge affects phase behavior. We adopt a mapping from zeta potential (zeta) to the reduced Yukawa charge (q*), calibrated to experiments within a model oligomer-micelle mixture patterned on peptide amphiphile assemblies in the presence of dasiglucagon (DG). After identifying q(DG)  approximately  -6e as the effective DG charge required for LLPS, systematic variation of the micellar charge reveals a finite charge window bounded by lower and upper critical charges: increasing charge initially enhances micelle-polymer attraction and densifies the liquid complex, but at high charge, growing micelle-micelle repulsion destabilizes the dense phase. The predicted window overlaps the experimentally measured zeta values, and the zeta of glucose-associated PA-PBA lies within the island-like pocket, underscoring the dual regulatory role of electrostatics.

title: Contribution of disordered regions of the essential protein GEMIN5 to RNA binding.
authors: Francisco-Velilla, Rosario; Nahavandi Araghi, Azadeh; Ramajo, Jorge; Abellan, Salvador; Martinez-Salas, Encarnacion
abstract: GEMIN5 is emerging as a multifunctional RNA-binding protein (RBP) linked to human disease. This RBP comprises a WD40 repeat domain at the N terminus. The C-terminal region (G5C) includes a tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR)-like dimerization module, a non-canonical RNA-binding site (RBS), and an intrinsically disordered region (IDR). Understanding the molecular basis for RNA binding is critical to decipher how GEMIN5 pathological variants impact on their functions. Here we show that the RNA-binding domain consists of an extended binding surface comprising a serine-rich loop and an acidic cluster within the IDR. The RNA binding ability measured in vitro and in soluble cellular extracts indicated that individually, ser-rich motif and acidic cluster mutants diminished RNA binding intensity. However, in the absence of the RBS region, the TPR-extended protein is sufficient to facilitate RNA binding. AlphaFold modeling of the TPR-extended protein shows the assembly of an elongated dimer bound to RNA. The same RBS is observed in the G5C-RNA oligomer model. We propose that the elongated dimer forms an extended binding surface, fine-tuning the RNA binding ability of the G5C architecture.

title: The Disordome Paradigm: How Intrinsic Disorder Encodes Emergent Biological Function.
authors: Fantini, Jacques; Lefebvre, Marine; Aulas, Anais; Chahinian, Henri; Yahi, Nouara
abstract: Classical structural biology equates function with a fixed three-dimensional fold, a view challenged by intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and regions (IDRs), which populate broad conformational ensembles rather than a unique structure. This article introduces the "disordome" paradigm, extending Uversky's "unfoldome" to describe how function emerges from electrostatic and hydration landscapes that reshape reversibly upon encounter with a partner. Using alpha-synuclein binding to ganglioside-enriched rafts and IDR-driven liquid-liquid phase separation, we argue that transient folding-upon-binding events, potentially entropically cheap, generate information-rich complexes and condensates that dissolve once conditions change, consistent with the second law of thermodynamics. We trace this logic to overlooked precursors: in 1957 Klotz invoked rubber elasticity to introduce entropy as the driver of protein "disorientation", while in 1962 Bernal described such proteins as chains "coiled in different ways" and formulated a "two-atom rule" whereby bonding constraints fix atomic geometry only up to two atoms apart. We argue that the local under-determination described by this two-atom rule, left unresolved in IDPs by any conserved network of contacts, helps explain why AlphaFold fails on IDPs. A quantum-mechanical pillar (dispersion, OH-pi contacts, tunneling) is proposed as underrepresented in IDP research. We discuss implications for the origin of life, cellular regulation via condensates, and a therapeutic logic ("target the target, not the arrow") illustrated by AmyP53, which occupies raft gangliosides rather than disordered amyloid proteins in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases.

title: Drugging the Undruggable in Oncology: Structural Computation, Machine Learning, and Generative AI for Historically Intractable Targets.
authors: Stanczak, Mikolaj; Niazi, Sarfaraz
abstract: For four decades the central oncogenic drivers of human cancer the RAS GTPases, the transcription-factor MYC, mutant p53, and the protein-tyrosine phosphatases, fusion oncoproteins and intrinsically disordered regulators that surround them were regarded as undruggable: lacking deep, well-defined small-molecule binding pockets, governed by femtomolar substrate affinities, or driven through flat protein-protein interfaces that classical medicinal chemistry could not engage. The last decade has overturned that verdict. This narrative review argues that the convergence of three advances has made the undruggable proteome systematically approachable: the discovery of cryptic, allosteric and induced pockets through molecular dynamics and deep learning; the maturation of physics-based and machine-learned models that can read out binding from structure; and the rise in generative artificial intelligence that can design novel molecules conditioned directly on a three-dimensional target. We develop the argument in full formal detail. We set out the mathematics of modern molecular machine learning E(3)/SE(3)-equivariant graph neural networks, denoising diffusion and score-based generative models, and generative flow networks alongside the statistical mechanics of binding free energy (free-energy perturbation, thermodynamic integration, MM-PBSA), the kinetics of covalent inhibition, the equilibrium theory of ternary complexes and cooperativity that governs molecular glues and degraders, and the pharmacology that determines whether a designed molecule reaches and acts on a tumour. We then examine, target by target, the biology that made each oncoprotein intractable and the campaigns structural, chemical and increasingly computational that have begun to defeat it, distinguishing throughout what classical structural and computational work achieved, what machine learning demonstrably contributed, and what generative design has so far only promised: the switch-II pocket and the covalent KRAS-G12C and non-covalent KRAS-G12D and pan-RAS(ON) inhibitors; the mutation-created cavity of p53-Y220C and its first reactivators; the disordered MYC-MAX interface and the miniprotein Omomyc; and the allosteric tunnel of SHP2. These four are selected for mechanistic non-redundancy, on grounds we state explicitly, and the structured search framework and eligibility criteria underlying the review are documented. We foreground the newest evidence AlphaFold3, RoseTTAFold All-Atom, deep cryptic-pocket predictors, and the first generative-to-clinic existence proofs while maintaining candour about the field's hard limits: the physical-validity and generalisation gaps of deep docking, the bounded accuracy and cost of free-energy methods, the synthesizability gap, dual-use risk, and a clinical attrition that artificial intelligence has not yet reduced. The synthesis we offer is not that the problem is solved but that it has changed in kind: from a search for the rare tractable target to the deliberate, computable engineering of molecules against targets once thought beyond reach.

title: Unraveling Pectin-Protein Interactions in Milk-Based Cocoa Beverages: Molecular Docking and Microstructure.
authors: Akyil Ozturk, Saniye; Habibzadeh Khiabani, Arezou; Kamer, Deniz Damla Altan; Karaca, Ali Can; Konar, Nevzat; Simsek, Senay; Toker, Omer Said
abstract: This study investigated the synergistic effects of pectin concentration (0.038-0.462%) and homogenization pressure (5.85-34.1 MPa) on the physical and microstructural stability of milk-based cocoa beverages. A Central Composite Rotatable Design (CCRD) was employed to optimize these parameters by evaluating critical quality attributes, including water-holding capacity (WHC), sedimentation, creaming index, apparent viscosity, and colloidal stability. To elucidate the underlying stabilization mechanisms, molecular docking simulations were integrated to assess the thermodynamic binding affinities between pectin (D-galacturonic acid) and major milk proteins. Numerical optimization identified 0.40% pectin and a homogenization pressure of 10 MPa as the optimal formulation and processing conditions. Under these conditions, the beverage achieved a maximum WHC of 86.04%, complete elimination of macroscopic phase separation (n.d. sedimentation and creaming), and an apparent viscosity of 67.39 mPa.s. Mechanistically, molecular docking revealed strong, multifaceted hydrogen-bonding and electrostatic interactions between pectin and milk proteins, with beta-lactoglobulin exhibiting the strongest predicted thermodynamic binding affinity (-6.3 kcal/mol). This macromolecular complexation promoted pronounced steric and electrostatic stabilization, as supported by the highly negative zeta potential (-30.8 mV) and enhanced microstructural uniformity observed through scanning electron microscopy-energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDS) analysis. A rigorous 9-month storage study further demonstrated prolonged kinetic stability. Structural integrity was largely maintained, and macroscopic phase separation was substantially delayed despite time-dependent rheological rearrangements during storage. Furthermore, sensory profiling demonstrated high consumer acceptability, particularly for smoothness and homogeneity, with the optimized formulation outperforming the evaluated commercial counterparts. Collectively, these findings demonstrate the effectiveness of pectin in such beverage system and provide practical formulation and processing strategies for improving the physicochemical stability and shelf life of complex dairy-based dispersions.

title: Negative Interfacial Tension Driven by Intrinsic Molecular Disorder.
authors: Tang, Chuan; Huang, Yifan; Ren, Chun-Lai; Tang, Qiyun; Ma, Yu-Qiang
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Intrinsically disordered molecular systems, such as random copolymers and intrinsically disordered proteins, exhibit scale-invariant, power-law cluster distributions that cannot be explained by conventional mean-field theories. A fundamental challenge is to understand how sequence randomness, which cannot be averaged into effective parameters, drives the formation of such polydisperse assemblies. Using a minimal coupled field theory that explicitly links a conserved density field to a nonconserved "junction" field representing stochastic binding site density, we show that the attraction between two fields chi, together with the fluctuations in the junction field Tϵ, renormalizes the effective interfacial tension to negative values: Deltagamma  approximately  -Tϵchi2. This negative interfacial tension suppresses coalescence and stabilizes a scale-invariant ensemble of clusters with a power-law size distribution, as confirmed by both numerical calculations and coarse-grained simulations of sequence-disordered biomolecules, and are consistent with diverse experimental observations. Our work reveals a general physicochemical mechanism by which intrinsic molecular disorder and fluctuations jointly govern phase separation in systems with built-in randomness, providing a unifying, chemistry-oriented framework for understanding and engineering heterogeneous soft matter systems.

title: Calculation of salt solubility in aqueous electrolyte solutions based on a thermodynamic ion-aggregation model.
authors: Tun, Lykoung; Ryu, Jonghyuk; Choi, Kanghyeon; Kim, Chanhui; Hwang, Seungeui; Choi, Jun-Ho
abstract: Based on a thermodynamic self-association model in salt solutions, new attempts have been made to predict salt solubility in NaCl solutions and other electrolyte solutions by incorporating potential of mean force (PMF) analysis from molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. It was demonstrated that salt solubility is closely associated with critical ion aggregation concentration (CIAC) in the thermodynamic ion aggregation process. The CIAC is determined by estimating effective binding energy between a cation and an anion or a mean equilibrium constant in ion association process. The calculated salt solubilities in various alkali halide solutions are consistent with the experimentally measured values. Combined MD simulations and graph-theoretical analysis revealed that, in NaCl solutions, most ions remain isolated at lower salt concentrations, whereas various-sized ion aggregates emerge as the salt concentration increases. As the salt concentration rises beyond the CIAC, large aggregates are formed, eventually leading to liquid-solid phase separation in NaCl-water mixtures. It is anticipated that this salt solubility prediction approach, based on the thermodynamic ion self-association model, may also contribute to estimating the solubility limit of various solute molecules in aqueous solutions, such as alcohols, osmolytes, and peptides.

title: PED in 2027: integrating experimental and predicted protein conformational ensembles at scale.
authors: Monzon, Alexander Miguel; Ghafouri, Hamidreza; Castro, Ximena Aixa; Khezrian, Sina; Aspromonte, Maria Cristina; Singla, Kavita; Barethiya, Shrishti; Bernado, Pau; Bonomi, Massimiliano; Chen, Jianhan; Cordeiro, Tiago; Cortes, Juan; De Castro, Stefano; Emenecker, Ryan; Feig, Michael; Forman-Kay, Julie D; Head-Gordon, Teresa; Holehouse, Alex; Janson, Giacomo; Lindorff-Larsen, Kresten; Liu, Zi Hao; Longhi, Sonia; Pajkos, Matyas; Robustelli, Paul; Rodriguez, Santiago; Schnapka, Vincent; Sibille, Nathalie; Vendruscolo, Michele; Tosatto, Silvio C E
abstract: The Protein Ensemble Database (PED; https://proteinensemble.org) is the primary deposition resource for structural ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). PED 2027 (released in September 2026) substantially expands its scope by integrating ensembles determined or refined using experimental data with clearly identified collections of computational predictions. The release introduces a multi-method collection targeting 3319 DisProt proteins and 2452 manually curated disordered regions, together with AlphaFlex ensembles for 10 022 human proteins containing IDRs. Alternative predictions for the same sequence are retained as independent records with method-specific provenance, enabling comparison across ensemble-generation approaches. A scalable deposition workflow accommodates individual experimental studies and proteome-scale collections while preserving quality control and curator oversight. The PED controlled vocabulary standardizes experimental data acquisition, computational generation, selection, and refinement. Precomputed IDPEnsembleTools and CIDER analyses provide structural and sequence-derived descriptors directly on ensemble pages. A redesigned interface and extended REST API support discovery, visualization, download and programmatic access. Interoperability with UniProt, DisProt, MobiDB, and experimental-data repositories connects ensembles with sequences, annotations, and supporting measurements. PED 2027 therefore provides an interoperable, analysis-ready platform for studying IDP/IDR conformational behaviour.

title: Inside biomolecular condensates: the interplay between physicochemical environments and molecular partitioning.
authors: Andre, Alain A M
journal: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Proteins and proteomics
abstract: Biomolecular condensates are protein- and nucleic acid-rich assemblies that compartmentalise cellular chemistry without a surrounding membrane. While much attention has focused on the molecular interactions driving their formation, condensates also establish distinct physicochemical microenvironments that influence their composition and function. In this mini-review we discuss how ions, solvent properties, small metabolites, and macromolecules shape condensate polarity, acidity, viscosity, hydration, electrochemical potential, and molecular mobility. We further discuss how these environments govern the selective partitioning of small molecules and macromolecules, and how recruited molecules can in turn reshape the condensate itself. An expanding experimental toolbox is beginning to quantify these reciprocal relationships and reveal condensates as crowded, chemically selective aqueous phases rather than passive compartments. Establishing quantitative relationships between condensate composition, microenvironment, and molecular partitioning may ultimately enable prediction of how these assemblies regulate biochemical processes in cells.

title: beta motifs and molecular flux promote fibril growth at condensate interfaces.
authors: Biswas, Subhadip; Potoyan, Davit A
abstract: Biomolecular condensates can age into gel-like or solid-like states, and their interfaces can promote amyloid fibril formation. Yet the physical principles selecting distinct interfacial aging pathways remain unclear. Here, we develop flux-driven molecular dynamics (FD-MD), a coarse-grained framework to disentangle the roles of rigid beta-prone motifs, hydrophobic sequence patterning and molecular deposition rate. We show that rigid motifs can sustain orientational order that converts interfacial adsorption into directional fibrillar growth, whereas flexible chains form spreading surface aggregates. Furthermore for fixed molecular architecture, changing the rate and manner of molecular delivery redirects assembly between lateral spreading, outward fibrillar growth, and bridging between opposing interfaces. Counterinutively, stronger initial drift toward the interface accelerates surface coverage but slows axial fibril elongation, consistent with competition between interfacial accumulation, orientational ordering and outward growth. Molecular architecture thus provides the capacity for directional assembly, while molecular supply selects it morphological outcome. Our findings provide a minimal physical framework for distinct condensate-aging pathwasy and suggest routes to redirect aging through molecular delivery and tuning of interfacial properties of condensates.

title: Targeting m6A Reader Phase Separation in Synaptic Plasticity: A Hypothesis-Generating Framework for Epitranscriptomic Drug Discovery.
authors: Rastmanesh, Reza
abstract: Epitranscriptomic drug discovery has mostly targeted the catalytic "writers" (METTL3/METTL14) and "erasers" (FTO, ALKBH5) that deposit and remove N6-methyladenosine (m6A). That strategy just hit clinical validation: STC-15, a METTL3 inhibitor, has measurable anti-tumor activity from a first-in-human oncology trial, but the same structural features that made these enzymes attractive also limit them. Inhibition shifts m6A stoichiometry globally, while an m6A mark's functional impact depends almost entirely on cellular context. YTHDF family reader proteins offer another angle. Their low-complexity domains drive liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). m6A binding stimulates this condensation across YTHDF paralogs-a property that matters for therapeutic selectivity. We propose a Phase Transition Threshold model in which YTHDF2's condensation concentration decides whether synaptic mRNAs are degraded or maintained in translation-competent, FMRP-associated states. Recent evidence has established YTHDF2 synaptic localization, FMRP condensate formation in neurons, and functional antagonism between the two proteins. The central unresolved question is whether condensation in living cells is nucleation-driven rather than bulk-concentration-driven. If so, concentration-centered pharmacology misses the point. We present falsifiable predictions and a staged experimental program. A more fundamental risk is that YTHDF2-mediated decay may not require condensate formation at all. If that is the case, the therapeutic premise of this Perspective collapses.

title: Beyond Equilibrium Ensembles: Time Rescaling in Coarse-Grained Simulations across Single-Molecule and Condensate Regimes.
authors: Gopi, Soundhararajan; Qin, Hanling; Best, Robert B; Schuler, Benjamin
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Residue-level coarse-grained simulations provide a powerful route for modeling biomolecular condensates over length and time scales that are difficult to access with atomistic molecular dynamics. Coarse-grained models have been shown to reproduce many aspects of equilibrium phase behavior. However, it remains unclear to what extent such models can reproduce the relative timescales of molecular dynamics. Here, we examine this question for complex coacervates with markedly different dynamics, formed by the highly acidic intrinsically disordered protein prothymosin alpha with four cationic partners: linker histone H1, protamine, polylysine, and polyarginine. Coexistence simulations using a residue-level coarse-grained model reproduce key equilibrium observables from experiments, including dense-phase concentrations, ionic-strength-dependent phase behavior, and chain dimensions in the dense and dilute phases. Dynamics are accelerated in these simulations, but a composition-specific time-rescaling factor captures the ionic-strength dependence of chain reconfiguration times within a given complex coacervate. In contrast, time rescaling is not transferable between dense and dilute phases or across condensate compositions and can depend on the chosen observable. These results show that agreement with measured equilibrium observables does not imply a universally transferable timescale for conformational dynamics in residue-level coarse-grained simulations. However, we find that the required time rescaling strongly correlates with the interaction energy of the protein chains, suggesting that the missing frictional effects arise from protein-protein interactions rather than solely from protein-solvent interactions, reminiscent of internal friction. Our findings highlight the need to combine thermodynamic validation with kinetic calibration when interpreting chain relaxation, molecular diffusion, and material properties from residue-level coarse-grained simulations of biomolecular condensates.

title: Hydrophobic Patch Spacing Produces Nonmonotonic Compaction in Intrinsically Disordered Proteins.
authors: Silvernail, Henry; Yang, Wangfei; Zheng, Wenwei
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: The conformational ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are encoded by the distribution of physicochemical interactions along their sequences. Although hydropathy-based descriptors capture average chain dimensions across diverse IDPs, the consequences of spacing localized hydrophobic patches remain poorly understood. Coarse-grained simulations of fixed-composition FUS-derived sequence variants reveal maximal compaction at an intermediate patch spacing. Analysis of simplified model peptides identifies this nonmonotonic behavior as one of three spacing responses: monotonic expansion, nonmonotonic compaction, and monotonic compaction. Their occurrence depends on interaction strength, effective interaction length scale, and patch architecture, with nonmonotonicity emerging only when hydrophobic attractions are sufficiently strong. A conformational-class decomposition resolves these responses into weighted patch-contact and patch-noncontact contributions to the ensemble-averaged chain dimensions. In attractive regimes, the contact contribution decreases with spacing while the noncontact contribution increases, and the changing balance between these opposing effects produces maximal compaction at an intermediate spacing. In the steric-dominated regime, separating the patches instead compacts the dominant noncontact conformations by relieving steric frustration. These steric-and attraction-dominated limits show that similar spacing responses can arise from distinct microscopic mechanisms. These findings establish a unified framework for understanding how interaction regime and hydrophobic patch spacing jointly shape IDP conformational ensembles.

title: Scaffold Affinity Tunes Biomolecular Condensate Function.
authors: Reyna, Andres; Briggs, Madyson O; Russell, Alexander F; Phan, Tien M; Wang, Ryan J; Allen, Reuben; Hinds, Thomas R; Zheng, Ning; Mittal, Jeetain; Chatterjee, Champak
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Biomolecular condensates (BMCs) organize cellular biochemistry by concentrating selected molecules into dynamic membrane-free compartments. Yet the molecular parameters that determine not only whether condensates form, but also how they behave and what they do, remain poorly defined. Here we show that scaffold binding affinity (K (d) ) is a quantitative determinant of condensate phase behavior, internal dynamics and biochemical output. Using a modular SUMO-SIM system in which scaffold valency was held constant while binding affinity was systematically varied, we found that affinity governs the phase boundary, resistance to chemical perturbation, and molecular mobility of condensates in vitro and in human cells. In multicomponent mixtures, the highest-affinity scaffold dominated dense-phase composition and dynamics, revealing a hierarchical rule for condensate organization. Finally, affinity-dependent changes in condensate dynamics translated into tunable enzyme activity, establishing binding energetics as an engineerable parameter for programming condensate biochemistry.

title: N6-Methyladenosine RNA Modifications Influence the Stability of FUS-Dependent Biological Condensate Formation.
authors: Thalagaha Mudiyanselage, Chamali; Pandey, Milan; Abedeera, Sudeshi M; Ekanayake, Chathurani; Mollah, Aftab U; Anwaar, Nadia; Konar, Arkaprabha; Abeysirigunawardena, Sanjaya C
abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) is a process in which proteins and nucleic acids organize into dynamic, membrane-less structures within cells. These structures help regulate cellular processes such as gene expression, molecular storage, and stress responses through weak interactions between disordered protein regions and RNA. Emerging evidence highlights a regulatory role for epitranscriptomic modifications, particularly N6-methyladenosine (m(6)A), though the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we investigated the relationship between m(6)A RNA nucleotide modification and LLPS by identifying proteins that selectively bind methylated RNA. An RNA pull-down assay enriched 106 proteins, including 53 known RNA-binding proteins and several proteins that support LLPS, including FUS (Fused in sarcoma). FUS, a well-characterized phase-separating RNA-binding protein, showed a 2-fold higher binding affinity for m(6)A-modified hairpin RNA than for its unmodified counterpart. Cloud-point analysis and coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS) microscopy revealed enhanced thermodynamic stability at higher m(6)A levels in total RNA extracts. Quantitative CARS imaging revealed that, although the overall RNA-to-protein ratio within condensates remains largely unchanged, larger droplets under high-m(6)A conditions exhibit increased RNA content, suggesting that m(6)A strengthens RNA-protein interactions without significantly altering the stoichiometry. Collectively, these findings indicate that while protein-protein interactions may initiate LLPS, m(6)A-modulated RNA-protein interactions govern condensate growth and stability. Furthermore, these results provide a mechanistic insight into how epitranscriptomic modifications regulate biomolecular condensation and influence cellular organization, gene regulation, and disease processes.

title: De novo Protein Generating Model via Structure-Aware Graph Neural Networks
authors: Chance M Gammill; Lakshman Tamil
abstract: The focus of this paper is to create a protein conformation prediction model that is optimized for structural accuracy rather than sequence recovery. To achieve this goal, we created a graph neural network (GNN) [19] for the design of computational proteins that integrates differentiable structure prediction through ESMFold [13] via a structural loss function, allowing direct optimization of the 3D conformational accuracy. Our model takes protein backbone coordinates as input and predicts an amino acid sequence using a composite loss that heavily weights structural similarity. On a matched evaluation sample, our model achieves structural precision (RMSD, TM-score, and GDT-TS) that is statistically indistinguishable from ProteinMPNN, a leading sequence recovery-focused method, despite training with no direct sequence recovery supervision and substantially lower native sequence recovery. Our results demonstrate that sequence recovery is not necessary to achieve competitive structural accuracy and that proteins can possess multiple non-unique solutions, suggesting that protein sequence prediction models may perform comparably well under purely structural conformation training. This distinction in training data and model structure allows for the training of a protein-generating model on non-natural proteins. Creating a model designed for de novo protein generation.

title: Building synthetic cell-cell synapses using engineered scaffold protein condensates
authors: Shin NY; Mitra G; Grodsky AM; Ruff KM; Chauhan G; Pappu RV; Lim WA
abstract: Synaptic assemblies that form at cell-cell junctions are often organized by multivalent scaffold proteins with condensate forming properties. An emerging hypothesis is that these scaffolds provide a thresholding mechanism whereby small increases in the density of cell-cell recognition receptors can trigger all-or-none assembly selectively at the correct partner cell interface. We test this hypothesis by engineering synthetic scaffolded synapses. Coarse-grained simulations suggest that properly-tuned scaffold interactions can yield a sharp condensation threshold. Guided by these simulations, we designed modular scaffold proteins consisting of PDZ domains and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of different molecular grammars. Within a specific region of parameter space, controlled by valency, receptor binding affinity and IDR-driven condensation, the synthetic scaffold proteins exhibit switch-like condensation behaviors, where co-condensates of receptor and scaffold selectively form only at interfaces with the proper partner cell. Notably, orthogonal receptor-scaffold pairs enable a single receiver cell to form multiple distinct interfaces, each associated with a different partner cell. We demonstrate that these synthetic synapse assemblies can recruit different client proteins to enhance intercellular signaling, orient cell division, or sculpt complex synaptic morphologies. Our results illustrate how the ultrasensitive condensation properties of modular scaffold proteins can be harnessed to create novel and highly specific cell-cell interfaces.

title: NMR-measured Per-residue Electrostatic Potentials Reveal the Importance of Arginine-Lysine Balance on the Conformational Ensemble of Disordered Histone H3 Tails in Nucleosome Core Particles
authors: Estelle AB; Schnapka V; Bolik-Coulon N; Bonomi M; Kay LE
abstract: Biophysical studies of chromatin have provided key insights into how the genome is regulated. Many atomic resolution structures of the fundamental building block of chromatin, the nucleosome core particle (NCP), as well as larger NCP arrays, both in isolation and in complex with effectors, or with post-translational modifications, have been elucidated. These provide in-depth pictures of key functional interactions. Considerably less information is available on the intrinsically disordered nucleosome tails that are critically important for higher order interactions in chromatin, and for transcription, DNA repair, and phase separation, and that serve as hubs for post-translational modifications. Here we focus on the tail of one of the four histones, histone-3 (H3), and measure electrostatic potentials at each of its amide proton positions in isolated NCPs via solution NMR spectroscopy. Using these potentials, in concert with molecular dynamics simulations, an ensemble of structures is calculated for WT H3 tails, as well as variants where all tail arginines are replaced by lysines (R2K) or vice versa (K2R). Our ensembles reveal that K2R tails have a higher propensity to occupy the most negatively charged region of the NCP between the DNA gyres than R2K or WT tails, while lysine enriched tails have an increased relative preference for the less negative regions near the DNA entry and exit points. The structural ensembles provide insight into differences in interactions between neighboring particles that lead to changes in diffusion and phase separation propensities between the NCP variants.

title: Comparative Analysis of Basic Machine Learning and Rigorous Free-Energy Calculation on Benchmarking Datasets of Protein-Ligand Binding Affinity
authors: Stefan J. P. Chrin; Gregory A. Landrum; Sereina Riniker
abstract: Rigorous free-energy methods based on molecular dynamics simulations like free-energy perturbation (FEP) are nowadays widely applied in lead optimization in pharmaceutical companies. Due to sampling restrictions and potential force-field deficiencies, it is common practice to first validate the applicability of FEP to a target/chemical series using a small number of known compounds, before applying it prospectively. As rigorous methods require significant computational resources, we want to explore how basic machine learning (ML) methods perform under the same conditions, i.e., training on a small number of known compounds and estimating the affinity of novel variants in the same chemical series. We apply classical ML models using 2D and 3D molecular descriptors, alongside two implementations of 3D quantitative structure–activity relationship modeling, and integrate the predictions through meta-learning. For many of the standard benchmarking datasets, we find that one of the ML models matches or exceeds the performance of FEP. Interestingly, ML-based predictions generally exhibit flatter slopes in parity plots, but without substantial effect on the relative rank ordering of compounds. Given their lower computational cost and ease of deployment, basic ML methods, particularly the meta-learner, emerge as a powerful complement to rigorous free-energy methods for estimating binding affinities within chemical series.

title: Foldability Is an Intrinsic Property of Protein Sequences: A Lattice Model Study with Information-Theoretic Approach and Unsupervised Machine Learning
authors: Shubin Liu
abstract: Protein structure prediction has been largely solved, but why a given sequence is foldable has not. We address this question for 27-, 48- and 64-residue lattice heteropolymers with statistical thermodynamics, the informationtheoretic approach (ITA) and a variational autoencoder (VAE). Native populations, folding probabilities and freeenergy surfaces are reproducible and independent of the initial denatured ensemble, so foldability is an intrinsic property of the sequence at a given temperature and solvent. We then ask where the observed regularities come from. Stability is governed by an information balance: the information content (self-information) of the native energy relative to the maximum-entropy description of compact alternatives, ℐtail, must exceed their Shannon entropy, 𝑆c = ln𝛺c. This is the random-energy-model condition for a folding transition, and ℐtail/𝑆c fixes the ratio of folding to glass temperatures, recasting minimal frustration in information units. Foldable sequences have smooth funnels, minimal Shannon entropy and minimal Fisher information in the native state, and a single sharp maximum of Fisher information at melting (cooperativity). Mutual and conditional information show that stability is an approximately sufficient statistic for kinetic accessibility of compact 27-mers. No hierarchical folding order is found. Variational autoencoders trained without labels distinguish sequences by their folding ensembles, supply a six-variable reaction coordinate that retains 91% of the kinetic information in the full native-contact map, and rediscover the native energy gap from the density of compact states.
